title: “They Are Not Here for the Camera”: Community-level strategies for building climate‑resilient health systems in response to floods in Uganda
content:
by Adelaine Aryaija-Karemani, Justine Namakula, Hakimu Sseviiri, Revocatus Twinomuhangi, Susannah Mayhew, Freddie Ssengooba, PARES Consortium

Climate-related shocks pose challenges to community health systems. Limited evidence exists on how to build resilience in these systems, especially regarding governance and community engagement and involvement (CEI). This study examined how communities in flood-prone Uganda enhance community health system resilience. We conducted a qualitative case study in Kasese and Katakwi districts using 12 focus group discussions and 46 key informant interviews with community members, health workers, local leaders, government officials and representatives of community-based, and non-governmental organizations. Data were analyzed thematically, guided by Blanchet’s health systems resilience governance dimensions: knowledge integration, anticipation and uncertainty management, interdependence, and legitimacy/institutional adaptation. Analytical induction explored CEI’s role in building absorptive, adaptive, and transformative resilience capacities. Community resilience was co-produced through interactions across governance dimensions, underpinned CEI. Communities demonstrated absorptive capacity by combining indigenous and scientific knowledge to anticipate flood risks, disseminate early warning, and implement risk pooling and social safety-net strategies like food banks and savings groups. Adaptive capacity was evident in the collaboration and interdependence between community structures, NGOs, and local government authorities that enabled responses and flexible programming. Transformative capacity was achieved through participatory governance structures and sustained engagement, which strengthened legitimacy but remained vulnerable to political pressures. CEI was critical across resilience capacities., providing trusted channels for information exchange, mobilizing collective action, and bridging realities and formal governance systems. In flood-prone Uganda, community agency and participatory governance structures are central to climate-resilient community health systems. Strengthening resilience requires embedding CEI within disaster governance processes by supporting hybrid knowledge systems, fostering anticipatory action, and promoting legitimate, adaptive institutions. CEI, knowledge co-production, and institutional flexibility are crucial strategies for building climate-resilient community health systems. These strategies should inform policy and practice in similar regions to strengthen adaptive capacity, build trust, and ensure equitable, sustainable health responses to climate shocks.
